text: Done. Report

attached, tree structured, status set to `needs_review`.

**What I found:**
The 50-state picture collapses to a much simpler shape than the brief assumed.
Only three states have dedicated biometric statutes (IL, TX, WA); about 17 more
treat biometrics as sensitive data requiring opt-in under comprehensive privacy laws; the rest only have
breach notification. **Build the consent flow to the Illinois standard and it clears all 50 states** — there's only

one build to do.

**The genuinely dangerous state is Illinois, and only Illinois.** It's the sole state with a private right of action for cons
ent defects, no injury required (*Rosenbach*), with fee-shifting. The 2024 SB 2
979 amendment killed the per-scan multiplier — and the 7th Circuit made that retroactive in April 2

026 — but headcount × $1,000 plus fees is still the exposure.

Texas is second:
AG-only, but that AG has collected ~$2.8B from Meta and Google. I checked whether the new HB 149

AI exemption helps us — it doesn't, it expressly falls away when the system identifies a specific individual.

**

Three things worth your attention:**

1. **The template-deletion question is the highest-leverage control in the project.** If eng
ineering can delete the face template the moment the match succeeds, BIPA's 3-year clock, CUBI's 1-year deadline,
Colorado's retention duty and most of the California breach exposure all shrink simultaneously. I'd

ask that before anything else — it may change the Illinois decision.
2. **California is a breach-
risk state, not a consent-risk state.** The private right of action there only opens on a breach with inadequate security, so the control that

matters is encryption, not consent copy. Worth not over-investing in the wrong place.
3. **I
didn't decide the Illinois launch question** — that's a risk-appetite call with real money on it

, not mine to make.

Two drafting subtasks (consent screen copy, public retention policy) are assig

ned to me and ready whenever you want them. The vendor DPA, DPIA, and counsel review need a human.

One caveat I've put in the report and
the comment: this is research to scope the work, not legal advice. Don't launch a face-scan sign
up on it alone — the counsel-review subtask has four specific questions to put to a privacy lawyer, including one I couldn't resolve c
leanly (whether NYC's biometric ordinance reaches a mobile-only app with no physical premises).
